The premise

Admin gets control. The client gets clarity.

Agencies run projects across email threads, spreadsheets, and calls — and clients are left guessing. The brief was strict about scope: no CRM, no kanban board, no invoicing engine. Just the smallest product that answers nine questions a client actually has, and nothing an admin doesn't need.

Admin

Runs the engagement

Full control over every client, project, price, and document — without touching code.

  • Create clients, projects, services & pricing
  • Post updates, schedule meetings, track milestones
  • Control exactly what each client can see
  • Set client logins directly — no self-service reset
Client

Sees exactly what matters

Nine questions answered in seconds, every time they log in.

  • What did we buy, and what's it costing us?
  • What's done, what's happening, what's next?
  • What do you need from me, and when do we meet?
Admin portal

Everything the agency needs, nothing it doesn't

01 — 04
01

A dashboard that surfaces what needs attention

No vanity charts. Four numbers that matter, computed live from real records — never a stored, staleable field — plus a "Needs Attention" feed that pulls together overdue payments, pending client actions, and fresh client requests from across every account.

  • Outstanding = project value minus paid, calculated on every request
  • Recent activity merged from five different tables into one timeline
  • Upcoming meetings pulled by nearest future date, never hand-entered
admin-client-portal.sumukhai.io
02

Every client, one accountable view

The client list and profile roll up active projects, total contract value, and outstanding balance — all derived, never duplicated. Internal notes stay internal; nothing marked private ever reaches the client-facing queries, enforced at the data layer, not just hidden in the UI.

admin-client-portal.sumukhai.io/clients/aurora
03

One page, the entire project lifecycle

This is the busiest screen in the product, and deliberately so: milestones, services with editable inclusions, payment history, a client-visible update log, business goals split from the rest of the requirements, meetings, deliverables, client actions, incoming client requests, and documents — all in one place, each section independently editable inline.

  • Reorderable milestone timeline — no hardcoded phase names
  • Business goals surfaced separately so they never get buried
  • Requirement edits version instead of overwriting history

04

Retainers and one-off projects, in either currency

Not every engagement itemizes by service. A project can carry an explicit deal amount — a monthly retainer or a one-time fee, in INR or USD — which silently overrides the sum of service prices wherever "project value" is shown. No itemization required for a blended retainer figure.

The whole relationship, above the fold

Status, current phase, this week's activity, next meeting, and a one-line count of anything pending — with a button into the full list, not a wall of detail dropped on the homepage. The client scans it in under ten seconds.

Scope and spend, in plain language

Business goals up top — so the client can see we're building toward what we actually agreed on — then services with what's included, and a single total investment figure that's always correct because it's computed, never re-typed.

A conversation that runs both directions

The admin can ask the client for something and get a written response back, not just a checkbox. The client can raise a request of their own — it shows up in the agency's "Needs Attention" feed within one request-response cycle, deliberately kept one-way so it never grows into a chat feature.

Under the hood

Authorization is enforced at the data layer

A client changing an ID in the URL should never see another client's project. That constraint shaped the architecture from the first migration — every query that returns client-facing data filters by the session's own clientId, never a value the request supplies.

architecture
01

Edge-level route gate

Middleware blocks unauthenticated access to /admin/* and /client/*, and bounces a signed-in user out of the wrong portal — first line of defense, not the only one.

02

Every mutation re-checks the role

Thirty-plus server actions each call requireAdmin() or requireClient() independently. A client can't reach a pricing mutation even with a crafted request — it isn't hidden, it's rejected server-side.

03

Ownership asserted, not assumed

Client-side reads filter by session.clientId and assert project ownership before rendering. A mismatch 404s — it doesn't even confirm the record exists.

04

Visibility flags, respected everywhere

CLIENT_VISIBLE vs INTERNAL_ONLY governs requirements, meetings, documents, and updates — checked in the query itself, so an internal note can never leak through an API response.

05

Client passwords, admin-controlled only

A deliberate call: clients can't self-reset. Only the admin can set a client's password, from a dedicated panel — shown right, with a one-time reveal.

06

Role-restricted custom domains

client-portal. and admin-client-portal. subdomains each reject the wrong role's login at sign-in, with a message pointing to the correct one.

08

Client credentials never leave the admin's hands

No "forgot password" for clients, no self-service reset — that was a deliberate product call, not an oversight. Only the admin can set a client's password, generated or typed, revealed once for handing off directly.

admin-client-portal.sumukhai.io/clients/.../edit
Verified, not assumed

The security boundary was actually tested

Not "should work" — tested against the live deployment with real HTTP requests, simulating exactly the kind of ID-tampering a curious client might try.

verify.sh — run against production
$ curl client-A-session → /client/project/{client-B-project-id} → 404 — clean, no data leaked, existence not confirmed $ curl client-session → /api/documents/{internal-only-doc-id} → 403 — internal-only visibility enforced $ curl (no session) → /admin → 307 → /login — unauthenticated request blocked $ curl admin-session → /client (wrong portal for role) → 307 → /admin — bounced to the correct portal $ grep -r "requireAdmin" src/lib/actions/*.ts | wc -l → pricing, requirements & status mutations: admin-only, confirmed
Automation

The client hears about it without being asked to check

Post a client-visible update or raise a client action, and the client's login inbox gets a short, branded email — never their listed contact address, always the one they actually sign in with, so the link in the email always lands them on an account they can access. Internal-only activity never triggers a send, matching the same flag that already governs portal visibility. A failed send is logged and swallowed — it never blocks the action that triggered it.
